title: Jesus laid down his own soul
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τοῦ Κλαζομενίου ὁ Κέλσος εἶπε προσθεὶς ἐπὶ τῆς κατ᾿ αὐτὸν ἱστορίας· μῶν οὐ τοῦτό φασιν, ὡς ἄρα ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ πολλάκις ἀπολιποῦσα τὸ σῶμα περιεπόλει ἀσώματος; καὶ οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἐνόμισαν θεὸν οἱ ἄνθρωποι. καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο φήσομεν ὅτι τάχα πονηροί τινες δαίμονες τοιαῦτα ᾠκονόμησαν ἀναγραφῆναι (οὐ γὰρ πιστεύω ὅτι καὶ γενέσθαι ᾠκονόμησαν). ἵνα τὰ προφητευθέντα περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὰ λεχθέντα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἤτοι ὡς πλάσματα ὅμοια ἐκείνοις διαβάλληται, η ὡς οὐδὲν πλεῖον ἑτέρων ἔχοντα μὴ πάνυ θαυμάζηται. ἔλεγε δὴ ὁ ἐμὸς Ἰησοῦς περὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῆς. οὐ κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον χρεὼν χωριζομένης τοῦ σώματος ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ καὶ περὶ τούτου παράδοξον ἐξουσίαν, τό· „οὐδεὶς αἴρει τὴν ψυχήν μου ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐγὼ τίθημι αὐτὴν ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ. ἐξουσίαν ἔχω θεῖναι αὐτὴν, καὶ πάλιν ἐξουσίαν ἔχω λαβεῖν αὐτήν.“ ἐπεὶ γὰρ „ἐξουσίαν“ εἶχε „θεῖναι αὐτὴν.“ ἔθηκε μὲν. ἡνίκα εἶπε· „πάτερ, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;“ καὶ „κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα,“ προλαβὼν τοὺς ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνασκολοπιζομένων δημίους. ὑποτέμνοντας τὰ σκέλη τῶν σταυρουμένων καὶ διὰ τοῦθ᾿ ὑποτέμνοντας, ἵνα μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον τιμωρίαν τίσωσιν. ἔλαβε δὲ „τὴν ψυχὴν“, ὅτε ἑαυτὸν ἐνεφάνισε τοῖς μαθηταῖς, προειπὼν ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν τοῖς ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ Ἰουδαίοις· „λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, κἀγὼ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν.“ καὶ „ἔλεγέ γε τοῦτο περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ.“ καὶ τῶν προφητῶν προκηρυξάντων τὸ τοιοῦτο διὰ πλειόνων καὶ διὰ τοῦ· „ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἡ σάρξ μου κατασκηνώσει ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι· ὅτι οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς τὸν ᾅδην οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν.“
pass_a_gloss: But since after these things Celsus also spoke about the Clazomenian (ὁ Κλαζομένιος), having added (προστίθημι) to the story (ἱστορία) about him: surely (μῶν οὐ) they say this, that then his soul (ψυχή) often (πολλάκις) leaving (ἀπολείπω) the body roamed about (περιπολέω) bodiless (ἀσώματος)? And not even him did men think (νομίζω) a god. And to this we shall say that perhaps some wicked (πονηρός) demons (δαίμονες) arranged (οἰκονομέω) such things to be written down (ἀναγράφω) (for I do not believe that they also arranged [them] to happen), that the things prophesied (προφητεύω) about Jesus and the things said by him might either as fictions (πλάσματα) like those be slandered (διαβάλλω), or as having nothing more than others not be much marvelled at (θαυμάζω). Now my Jesus said about his own soul, being separated (χωρίζω) from the body not according to the human necessity/debt (τὸ ἀνθρώπινον χρεών) but according to the extraordinary (παράδοξος) authority (ἐξουσία) given to him also about this, the [words]: no one takes (αἴρω) my soul from me, but I lay (τίθημι) it from myself; authority I have to lay it, and again authority I have to take (λαμβάνω) it. For since he had authority to lay it, he laid it, when he said: Father, why (ἱνατί) did you forsake (ἐγκαταλείπω) me? and crying (κράζω) with a great voice he let go (ἀφίημι) the spirit (πνεῦμα), anticipating (προλαμβάνω) the executioners (δήμιοι) [set] over those being impaled/crucified (ἀνασκολοπίζω), cutting under (ὑποτέμνω) the legs (σκέλη) of those being crucified (σταυρόω), and cutting for this, that they not pay (τίνω) punishment (τιμωρία) longer. And he took the soul when he showed (ἐμφανίζω) himself to the disciples, having foretold (προλέγω) before them (ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν) to the Jews disbelieving (ἀπιστέω) him: destroy (λύω) this temple (ναός), and I in three days will raise (ἐγείρω) it. And he said this about the temple of his body. And the prophets having proclaimed beforehand (προκηρύσσω) such a thing through more [places] and through this: and still also my flesh (σάρξ) will encamp (κατασκηνόω) in hope (ἐλπίς); for you will not forsake my soul into Hades (ᾅδης), nor give your holy one (ὅσιος) to see corruption (διαφθορά).
pass_b_english: Next Celsus also spoke of the man of Clazomenae and, on the story told of him, added: “Do they not say this, that his soul often left his body and wandered about without a body? And men did not think him a god either.” To this too we shall say that perhaps some wicked demons arranged for such things to be written down (for I do not believe that they also arranged for them to happen), so that the things prophesied about Jesus and the things said by him might either be slandered as fictions like those, or not be greatly marvelled at, as having nothing more than the others.

Now my Jesus said of his own soul, which was parted from the body not by the necessity common to men but by the extraordinary authority given to him over this also: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). For since he had “authority to lay it down,” he laid it down when he said, “Father, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34) and, “crying out with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit” (Matthew 27:50). In this he forestalled the executioners in charge of the crucified, who cut the legs of those crucified, and cut them for this reason, that they may not suffer punishment any longer (compare John 19:31–33).

And he took up “his soul” again when he showed himself to his disciples, having foretold it in their presence to the Jews who did not believe him: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). And “he was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:21). The prophets too had proclaimed such a thing beforehand in many places, and in this one: “Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope; for you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your Holy One see corruption” (Psalm 16:9–10; Acts 2:26–27).

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 32 (Koetschau 3.32). The man of Clazomenae is Hermotimus; he is not named in this chapter, so the English does not name him. Celsus’s words (μῶν οὐ τοῦτό φασιν … ἀσώματος; καὶ οὐδὲ τοῦτον ἐνόμισαν θεὸν οἱ ἄνθρωποι) are direct speech with finite verbs and are set in quotation marks; the second sentence is read as part of Celsus’s argument (it repeats his refrain from 3.26–31 that ‘no one thought him a god’). The opening ‘Ἐπεὶ δὲ … εἶπε’ (‘since Celsus spoke’) is a subordinate clause whose main clause is ‘φήσομεν’; it is broken into two sentences (‘Next Celsus also spoke … To this too we shall say’) without loss of sense. ψυχή is kept as ‘soul’ throughout, including in the quotation of John 10:18 (where English Bibles usually say ‘life’), because Origen’s argument turns on Jesus’ soul leaving the body, against the tale of Hermotimus’s roaming soul. Origen’s text of John 10:18 adds ‘τὴν ψυχήν μου’ (from 10:17) and places ‘πάλιν’ before ‘ἐξουσίαν’; translated as he gives it. The cry is given by Origen as ‘πάτερ, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;’ — ‘Father’, not the Gospels’ ‘My God, my God’ (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34); translated as Origen has it, cited to the Gospel verses. ‘κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ἀφῆκε τὸ πνεῦμα’ matches Matthew 27:50. The leg-breaking clause alludes to John 19:31–33 (the soldiers broke the legs of the two others but found Jesus already dead); cited inline with ‘compare’. ‘ὑποτέμνοντας τὰ σκέλη’ rendered ‘cut the legs’: ὑποτέμνω means to cut below, and Origen’s verb is kept rather than John’s ‘broke’ (κατέαξαν, John 19:32). ‘ἵνα μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον τιμωρίαν τίσωσιν’ rendered ‘that they may not suffer punishment any longer’ (the breaking hastened death). ‘ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν’ is read as ‘in their presence’ (the disciples were present at John 2:19–22); it could also mean ‘about them’, but that fits the sentence poorly. The final period is a genitive absolute without a main verb in the staged text (καὶ τῶν προφητῶν προκηρυξάντων …); rendered as a finite sentence (‘The prophets too had proclaimed’). The prophecy is LXX Psalm 15:9–10, which is Psalm 16:9–10 in English Bibles; Origen’s wording ‘ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἡ σάρξ μου κατασκηνώσει ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι’ follows the LXX as quoted in Acts 2:26–27 (Origen has the article, ‘εἰς τὸν ᾅδην’, where the critical texts of LXX Psalm 15:10 and Acts 2:27 read ‘εἰς ᾅδην’). ‘ὅσιος’ (holy one) capitalised as ‘Holy One’ because Origen applies it to Christ.
